newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Slow boats from China signal end to Hong Kong era.
newsitem.headline: Slow boats from China signal end to Hong Kong era.

text.p: Relics of colonial rule are disappearing fast in Hong Kong, but for the last batch of British civil servants to cruise home before the handover, the remnants of empire are drifting away slowly.

Nearly 70 senior British civil servants plus their families left on a pair of slow boats from China this week, taking advangtage of a law that permits them to cruise home in style at taxpayers' expense.

The benefit dates back to the time before air travel and was dropped from new civil service contracts in 1984 after Hong Kong legislators objected to the cost -- about HK$60,000 (US$7,700) per person.
But the perk still exists for members of Her Majesty's Civil Service that joined before that date.
On Saturday evening, the luxury liner Queen Elizabeth 2 sailed from Hong Kong harbour with 16 civil servants and their dependants in the last such voyage before the handover.
Hong Kong reverts to China on midnight June 30 after more than 150 year of British colonial rule.
The even more opulent Oriana left on Thursday with more than 50 civil servants and 72 of their family members in tow.
Other government workers will take to the airways in coming months for a quicker but less glamorous route home.
Some of the departing civil servants found their jobs given to Hong Kong Chinese as part of a "localisation" policy, while others chose to leave rather than serve under the Chinese flag.

For some Hong Kong residents it was difficult to shed tears for British office workers that for years had enjoyed very comfortable lifestyles and were now entitled to a four-week free holiday at sea before returning home.
But for the affected civil servants, the leave-taking was bittersweet. Many had devoted their working lives to Hong Kong, raising their children here and, in some cases, marrying local residents.

"Naturally I am sad. We've been here nearly 18 years. Well, my wife has of course been here from birth. So it's a sad occasion," government lawyer Roy Griffey said as he prepared to board the Oriana on Thursday.
The departure of the two ships was another signal that Britain's hold on the territory is slipping away. Other signs have ranged from the symbolic to the significant.
One of the most obvious emblems of British domination made its final appearance in mid-January when Hong Kong's post office sold its last batch of stamps bearing Queen Elizabeth's profile.
In another swipe at empire, Hong Kong's Urban Council has decided to change the name of Victoria Park to the more neutral Hong Kong Central Park as part of the site's renovation.
But the statue of Queen Victoria will remain.

Justices of the peace, who have as their main duty the visiting of prisons, will no longer be asked to promise allegiance to the queen if a bill gazetted on Friday passes muster in Hong Kong's Legislative Council.
Instead, they will swear to "conscientiously and truly serve the people of Hong Kong".
On Wednesday, Britain will say goodbye to a more important element of its control in the territory when the government delivers the Hong Kong budget that straddles the handover.
The 1997/98 budget is the last in which Britain has a say in wealthy Hong Kong's money matters.
